133. Room (15), S wall, central section. Red middle area: painting with the torture of Dirce (72.5 x 66 cm).  The depiction of the myth of Dirce in the House of Menander, inserted in a wall of the first IV style (cf. wall E with Andromeda freed by Perseus and wall N with Perseus in the Palace of Kepheus), presents variations with respect to the traditional iconography of the myth, found in Pompeii and Herculaneum on walls of the final III style and of the IV style.  In fact, while Zeto holds - as usual - the bull by the horns, Amphion turns to speak with Hermes recognizable by the caduceus and the petasus. Along the slopes of the mountain in the background, a group of Bacchantes and Satyrs who are not represented in any other version of the subject under examination also agitates.  Also 1 three bodies of young men lying on the shields placed in the foreground are unusual and closely resemble, in the modest pictorial rendering, the sons of Laocoön depicted in the small picture on the S wall of the wing (4) (see fig. 68). 199. Lateral apside. Apse: paradeisos with Artemis and Actaeon torn to pieces by dogs; doors: plinth with plants; middle area with narrow compartment with candelabra surmounted by an eagle. The myth of Actaeon studied by Leach (Leach RM 1981, pp. 307-327, with a list of replicas in note 26), occurs with equal frequency on walls of the III and IV styles;  an example of the late II style is found in the blue monochrome from Herculaneum (Naples, National Museum, inv. 9413, Leach RM 1981, no. 20, fig. 132, 3). It has several versions that recur differently in the individual paintings. Sometimes the two moments - discovery and punishment - are depicted in a single painting; sometimes, especially in the replicas of the III style, the various moments of the myth are reproduced in narrative continuity. An element that constantly appears is Actaeon torn to pieces by dogs, while there are variations in the representation of the cause of punishment. As for the difference in representation between the mythological paintings of the III and IV styles, see those of the House of Venus in a bikini (I 11, 6). The myth became popular in Roman circles through literary sources and in particular Ovid (Met., 3, 138-252; Trisiah, 2, 105-106) whose account reflects the Callimachean source (Kall., Hymn., 5, 107-116). Later it finds its inspiration in Seneca (0ed., 751-763; Phoen., 12-16); Apuleius (Met., 2.4) and Statius (Silvae, 1.5.56; Thebaid., 3.202; 4.572574). The literary history of Actaeon shows the flexibility of the myth, which is therefore susceptible to individual interpretations. Pompeian paintings, and in particular those of ITI style, would refer to the Callimachean version (Leach RM 1981, p. 321). The author groups together a certain number of replicas, based on the choice of the events represented (Leach RM 1981, pp.313-323), but poorly represented by the myth offer too many compositional variants to be closely related. At the news that she would be asked by Scipio as a spoils of war, rather than see herself dishonored and BREOnIerS drank the poison offered to her by her husband.  The scene depicted in the painting takes place in a large colonnaded environment, adorned with curtains. In the center is placed a kline on which Sofonisba is lying with her left elbow resting while with her right hand she holds the cup filled with poison. Behind him a bearded man with a turban' (whom Elia NS 1934, p. 283 proposes to identify with Hasdrubal).  Around the klìne there are various other characters that are difficult to identify. A second representation, very similar in compositional scheme, comes, according to Schefold, from a room in the House of Joseph II, VIII 2, 39; but there is no certain information about its original location; it is now preserved in the National Museum of Naples (inv. 8968; Rizzo 1929, tav. 196). 29. Triclinium (9), W wall, central section. Middle area: aedicule with wings in perspective with a painting of the fall of Icarus (125 x 108 cm). The Fall of Icarus is part of that group of mythological-landscape paintings typical of the second phase of the III style; The elements of the myth are often arranged in continuous narration, within a fairytale landscape.  The myth has been studied by Blanckenhagen who identifies six replicas, nos. 5-10, including no. 7 from the triclinium (9) of the Blacksmith's House and traces its origin back to the painter of Boscotrecase. They are characterized by the complexity of the landscape background and the lack of a unitary perspective vision that is present in the depictions of the death of Icarus (Blanckenhagen nos. 1-4), probably dating back to a Hellenistic original transmitted to Pompeii from the painting of the Imperial Villa.  The painting of the Blacksmith's House has as its pendant the depiction of Paris on Mount Ida, or the judgment of Paris, also a frequent theme in the late III style. Of another pendani, later cut by a lararian niche, we can glimpse an idyllic-sacral PcHggio, which perhaps had, as Blanckenhagen proposes, Marsyas as its subject. The theme of Venus' toilet that appears in the cubicle (8) of the House of M. Lucretius Fronto follows the Hellenistic iconographic scheme inserted in the frieze of the Villa of the Mysteries of 50 BC. Venus appears seated on a throne, with one arm raised to arrange her hair, as in the painting of the Anadiomène of Apelles exhibited in the fourth century BC in the sanctuary of Asklepios at Cos and removed by Augustus to be placed in the temple of Divus Iulius in Rome (Strabo, XIV 2, 19; Plin., Nat. hist., XXXV, 91). As in the painting of the House on the First Floor, the painting of the House of M. Lucretius Fronto shows the dressing table of the goddess assisted by the Charites, who in our painting also hold the mirror, while in the painting of the House of M. Lucretius Fronto it is supported by Eros. The replica of the House on the First Floor also includes Mars, naked and unarmed, seated next to the shield.  The god is depicted according to the statuary type of the Ares Ludovisi, generally related to Pliny's information (Nat. hist., XXXVI, 26) about the group of Skopas in the Temple of Mars near the Circus Flaminius in Rome which included a seated Mars and a nude Venus. The temple founded by D. Junius Brutus Callaicus to commemorate the victory over the Challais in Lusitania in 133-132 BC, was restored by Augustus (see the diffusion of the image of the divine couple, progenitor of the gens /ulia, in the context of Augustan dynastic propaganda: cf. de Vos 1985, p. 362, note 3). The replica of the House on the First Floor which, especially in the Venus, fits into the popular trend of grapefruit painting, seems to be the mixture of two different cartoons, one that includes the dressing table of Venus attributable to the painting of Apelles, the other depicting Mars in the iconographic scheme of the Ares Ludovisi, to which according to the source mentioned above a statue of Venus was to be contrasted,  which, however, cannot be identified in the iconographic scheme of Venus' toilet. The replica, for the same reasons given for the painting with Theseus and Ariadne, is attributable to the final phase of the III style. (De Vos, 1985, pp. 360 ff).  And 103041
